Fallible means capable of making mistakes or being wrong.

If you describe someone or something as fallible, you are saying that they are not perfect — that errors, misjudgments, or failures are possible for them. It is the simple, honest recognition that something or someone is not immune to being wrong.

Think of it this way: a fallible person is not a bad person. They are simply a human person — one who can get things wrong, even when they are trying their best.

This is important, because learners often get this slightly wrong.

Fallible does not mean "always wrong" or "frequently wrong." It only means that being wrong is possible. A brilliant scientist can be fallible. A wise judge can be fallible. A loving, careful parent can be fallible. They may get things right 99% of the time — but because that remaining 1% of error is possible, they are still fallible.

So fallible is about potential, not frequency. It asks: Can this person or thing be wrong? If the answer is yes, they are fallible.
Who or What Can Be Fallible?

The word is flexible and can describe many things:

People — This is the most common use. Any human being can be called fallible, because all humans are capable of error. "Even the most experienced doctors are fallible." "He is a great leader, but a fallible one."

Human memory — Memory is notoriously fallible. Eyewitnesses to crimes often genuinely believe they remember things correctly, yet studies show that memory can distort, fill in gaps, or simply be wrong. "Human memory is fallible, which is why we write things down."

Judgment and reasoning — Our decision-making can be clouded by emotions, bias, or incomplete information. "Her judgment, however sharp, remains fallible."

Systems and institutions — Courts, governments, scientific processes, and technology can all be fallible. "No justice system is perfect — all are fallible to some degree."

Beliefs and knowledge — Even things we feel certain about can turn out to be wrong. "Our understanding of the universe is always growing, which means our current knowledge is fallible."
The Key Idea Behind the Word: No One is Exempt

The deeper truth that "fallible" captures is this — no person, no system, no institution is above the possibility of error. This is not a pessimistic idea. In fact, accepting fallibility is a sign of wisdom and intellectual maturity. The most dangerous people are often those who believe they cannot be wrong, because they stop checking themselves.

When someone openly acknowledges that they are fallible, it usually means they are humble, self-aware, and open to correction. These are good qualities.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Fallible is a relatively formal word. You would use it in essays, academic writing, thoughtful conversations, or anywhere you want to speak with precision. You would not typically say it in casual texting.

Its tone is neutral to slightly somber, but never harsh. It is not an insult. Saying "you are fallible" is not saying "you are incompetent" — it is saying "you are human, like the rest of us."

The direct opposite of fallible is infallible, which means incapable of being wrong or making mistakes. Something infallible cannot fail, cannot err, cannot be incorrect — ever.

In everyday language, "infallible" is sometimes used loosely to mean something that always works or is extremely reliable: "This method is not infallible, but it works most of the time." In religious contexts, it carries a stricter meaning — the Catholic Church, for example, holds that the Pope speaks infallibly on certain matters of doctrine.

Almost nothing in the real world is truly infallible. Recognising this is precisely why the word "fallible" exists and why it is so useful.

Here are varied, natural examples to show you how the word lives in real usage:

"We are all fallible — making mistakes is part of being human."

"The committee's decision was made by fallible people working with incomplete information."

"Science does not claim to have all the answers; it openly acknowledges that its conclusions are fallible and subject to revision."

"She trusted him, but she never forgot that even the best advisors are fallible."

"A fallible memory is not the same as a dishonest one — people can be genuinely wrong about what they remember."

"The system is clever, but not infallible — it makes errors under certain conditions."

To know that something or someone is fallible is to know this: perfection is not guaranteed here. Mistakes can happen. Errors are possible. This is not a flaw unique to bad people or broken systems — it is simply the condition of anything that exists in the real world and has to deal with complexity, uncertainty, and limitation.

Accepting fallibility — in yourself and in others — is the starting point of good thinking, honest science, fair judgment, and genuine humility.
